## **Previously on 201: Constituent and Its Types**
<br>
- **constituent**: a group of words that <span style="color:green"><b>acts together</b></span> as a **unit** <br><br>
- **phrases**: types of constituents, different types are decided by the **part of speech** of the **head**
<br><br>
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>noun phrase</b></span> (<span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span>): *<u>man</u>, the <u>man</u>, the happy <u>man</u>, the <u>man</u> with the hat*<br><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>prepositional phrase</b></span> (<span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span>): *<u>into</u> the forest, <u>by</u> the author, <u>for</u> good luck*<br><br>
  - **verb phrase** (<span style="color:#CC0033"><b>VP</b></span>): *<u>eats</u>, <u>eats</u> pizza, <u>eats</u> quickly, <u>eats</u> pizza quickly at noon*<br><br>
  - <span style="color:orange"><b>adjective phrase</b></span> (<span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span>): *<u>happy</u>, <u>ugly</u>*<br><br>
  - <span style="color:deeppink"><b>adverb phrase</b></span> (<span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span>): *<u>quickly</u>, <u>happily</u>*<br><br>
- **constituency tests**: to test whether a string of words is a constituent or not<br><br>
  - replacement, movement, fragment, coordination

# ***I saw the man with a telescope.***
<br><br>
### an example of **structural ambiguity**<br><br>
### but we did not look at it via **syntax trees** to visualize its two possible structures<br><br>
### the syntax trees on the previous page show how there are two ways to interpret what *<u>[with a telescope]</u>* **modifies**<br><br>
### the meaning of a sentence ≠ sum of its words, **syntactic structure** also contributes to meaning<br><br><br><br>
## HOW DO WE DRAW TREES THEN!

---
## **Phrase Structure Rules** (PSRs)
<br>
- there are (descriptive) rules that indicate **how phrases are built out of smaller units** (which could be words or other phrases)<br><br>
  - these rules are called **phrase structure rules** <br><br>
  - they indicate the order and position of the smaller units in a phrase <br><br>

- we derive these rules by observing what are the possible structures that exist in **natural language**<br><br>

.pull-left[
<br><br>
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b> → (D) (AdjP+) <b><span style="color:blue">N</span></b> (PP+)</h3>
]

.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/0930/teacher.png" width="70%">
]

---
## **Notational Notes**
<br>
phrase structure rules indicate the **order** and **position** of the sub-parts
<br><br>
.pull-left[
<img src="../pic/0930/notation1.png" width="90%">
]
.pull-right[
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b> → (D) (AdjP+) <b><span style="color:blue">N</span></b> (PP+)</h3><br>
<img src="../pic/0930/teachernode.png" width="100%">
]

---
## **Phrase Structure Rules for English**
<br>
.pull-left[
- <h3><b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b> → (D) (AdjP+) <b><span style="color:blue">N</span></b> (PP+)</h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:green">PP</span></b> → <b><span style="color:green">P</span></b> NP</h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:orange">AdjP</span></b> → (AdvP) <b><span style="color:orange">Adj</span></b></h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:deeppink">AdvP</span></b> → (AdvP) <b><span style="color:deeppink">Adv</span></b></h3><br>
]
.pull-right[
- <h3><b><span style="color:brown">TP</span></b> → NP <b><span style="color:brown">(T)</span></b> VP</h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:teal">CP</span></b> → <b><span style="color:teal">C</span></b> TP</h3><br>
]
- <h3><b><span style="color:#CC0033">VP</span></b> → (AdvP+) <b><span style="color:#CC0033">V</span></b> (NP) (NP) (AdvP+) (PP+) (AdvP+)</h3>

---
## **Noun Phrases (NP)**
<br>
.pull-left[
- a noun phrase consists of **a noun** and all the words that **modify** it<br><br>
- the simplest NP is a single noun:
  - *Harriet*, *dogs*, *soup*, *snow*<br><br>
- an <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> can also include any of the following:
  - a <span style="color:blue"><b>determiner</b></span><br>
  <i><span style="color:blue"><b>the</b></span> hat</i>, <i><span style="color:blue"><b>my</b></span> shoes</i>, <i><span style="color:blue"><b>this</b></span> idea</i>, <i><span style="color:blue"><b>which</b></span> tree</i><br><br>
  - one or more <span style="color:orange"><b>adjective phrases</b></span> (AdjP)<br>
  <i><span style="color:orange"><b>blue</b></span> sky</i>, <i>a <span style="color:orange"><b>great</b></span> time</i>, <i><span style="color:orange"><b>big red</b></span> trucks</i><br><br>
  - one or more prepositional phrases (PP)<br>
  <i>spaghetti <span style="color:green"><b>with meatballs</b></span></i>, <i>trees <span style="color:green"><b>in the yard</b></span></i>, <i>the tall bridge <span style="color:green"><b>over the river</b></span></i>
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/0930/nounph.jpg" width="90%">
]

- **note**: an adjective will **always** go in a separate AdjP, for reasons we'll discuss soon in a few pages later<br><br>

---
## **Phrase Structure Rules: Take NP as an Example**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **notational notes** once again:<br><br>
  - order **matters** – elements always appear in the order given in the rule<br><br>
  - parentheses = **optional** element<br><br>
  - no parentheses = **obligatory** element<br><br>
  - plus sign (+) = one or more<br><br>
- so the rule for <span style="color:blue"><b>noun phrases</b></span> means that a noun phrase consists of (in order):
  - optional determiner
  - one or more optional adjective phrase(s)
  - the <span style="color:blue"><b>noun</b></span>
  - one or more optional prepositional phrase(s)
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0930/notation1.png" width="60%">
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b> → (D) (AdjP+) <b><span style="color:blue">N</span></b> (PP+)</h3><br>
<img src="../pic/0930/teacher.png" width="60%">
</div>
]

## **Adjective Phrase (AdjP), Adverb Phrase (AdvP)**
<br>
.pull-left[
<img src="../pic/0930/well.jpg" width="80%">
]
.pull-right[
consider the following sentence, and think about whether <i><span style="color:#CC0033">happy</span></i> and <i><span style="color:green">quickly</span></i> are constituents?<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>The <i><span style="color:#CC0033">happy</span></i> dog ran <i><span style="color:green">quickly</span></i></i>.
</div>
<br>
- **constituency tests**:<br><br>
  - How was the dog who ran quickly? <i><span style="color:#CC0033">Happy</span></i>! (stand alone)
  - How did the happy dog run? <i><span style="color:green">Quickly</span></i>! (stand alone)
  - The happy dog ran like that. (replacing <i><span style="color:green">quickly</span></i>)<br><br>
- <b><span style="color:orange">adjectives</b></span> and <b><span style="color:deeppink">adverbs</b></span> are their own constituents, so they need to be put into their own phrases: <b><span style="color:orange">AdjP</b></span> and <b><span style="color:deeppink">AdvP</b></span>
]

---
## **Adjective Phrases (AdjP)**
<br>
.pull-left[
- most basic <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span>: one adjective (AdjP → Adj) <br>
  - it can be inserted into an <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> as shown on the right <br><br>
- **Modification Rule**
  - *a phrase that modifies a word must be a <b>sibling</b> of that word*
  - make a guess, what is this sibling?<br><br>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0930/slowcar.png" width="60%">
</div>
]<br>

--

.pull-left[
- by making the <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span> for <u><i>slow</i></u> a sibling of the **N** <u><i>car</i></u>, we're showing that *<u><i>slow</i></u>* modifies <u><i>car</i></u><br><br>
- we can verify they are siblings by checking they have the same **parent**: both the <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span> and the **N** <u><i>car</i></u> have <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> as parent
]
.pull-right[
]


---
## **Adjective Phrases (AdjP)**
<br>
.pull-left[
- <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span>s can optionally contain an <span style="color:deeppink"><b>adverb phrase</b></span>(<span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span>): <u><i>very slow</i></u><br><br>
- PSR for <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span> modified<br>
  **AdjP → (AdvP) Adj**<br><br>
- since the adverb modifies the adjective:
  - the adverb needs to go in its own <span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span>
  - that <span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span> needs to be a sibling of the adjective
  - that is, they need to be **children** of the same <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span><br><br>
  
- when there are **two** adjectives in one phrase:
  - they each is a separate <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span>
  - since both of them are modifying the **noun**
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0930/veryslowcar.png" width="50%">
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0930/longhair.png" width="70%">
</div>
]

---
## **Adverb Phrases (AdvP)**
<br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0930/adverb1.png" width="40%">
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0930/adverb2.png" width="40%">
</div>
]
.pull-right[
if we check the PSR rules for English <span style="color:deeppink"><b>adverb phrase</b></span> (<span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span>), we will notice that they are basically the same:<br><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:orange">AdjP</span></b> → (AdvP) <b><span style="color:orange">Adj</span></b></h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:deeppink">AdvP</span></b> → (AdvP) <b><span style="color:deeppink">Adv</span></b></h3><br><br>

- if you have two adverbs in a row, they will be in nested structure
  - the first one **modifies** the second
]

---
## **Prepositional Phrases (PP)**
<br>
.pull-left[
- the PSR for <span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span> is very straightforward<br><br>
- it is always a <span style="color:deeppink"><b>PP</b></span> containing the **head** P and an <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:green">PP</span></b> → <b><span style="color:green">P</span></b> NP</h3>
</div><br>
- other examples<br><br>
  - <i><span style="color:green"><b>in</b></span> the park</i>
  - <i><span style="color:green"><b>by</b></span> the tree</i>
  - <i><span style="color:green"><b>with</b></span> a friend</i>
  - <i><span style="color:green"><b>under</b></span> the sky</i>
  - <i><span style="color:green"><b>for</b></span> my mom</i>
  - ...
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0930/show.png" width="40%">
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0930/garden.png" width="60%">
</div>
]

---
## **Prepositional Phrases (PP)**
<br>
.pull-left[<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0930/gardenbench1.png" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
what's **noticeble** if we put these two PSRs together <br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:green">PP</span></b> → <b><span style="color:green">P</span></b> <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span></h3><br>
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b> → (D) (AdjP+) <b><span style="color:blue">N</span></b> (<span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span>+)</h3>
</div><br><br>

- <span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span> can contain <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span>, but <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> can contain <span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span> too<br><br>
- so we can have <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> and <span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span> nested to each other, go on and go on forever<br><br>
- this is an example of **recursion**, which is an important feature of human language
]

<br>

  - recall the **modification rule** – a phrase that modifies a word must be its **sibling**
